title: Rice Grassy Stunt: How to Spot It and Protect Your Palay
metaTitle: Rice Grassy Stunt: Signs, Damage and Control
metaDescription: Rice grassy stunt makes palay plants short, grassy and yellow, with no panicles. Learn the signs, the planthopper link and the steps that protect you.
excerpt: Rice grassy stunt is a virus disease that turns palay plants into short, yellowish, grass like clumps that rarely make a panicle. There is no cure, so the whole game is stopping the brown planthopper that carries it.

heroImage.alt: A brown planthopper on a rice leaf. This insect spreads rice grassy stunt from plant to plant
heroImage.credit: portioid, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Rice grassy stunt comes from the Rice grassy stunt virus. The [brown planthopper](/pests/brown-planthopper) spreads it, both as a young nymph and as an adult. This disease is found where rice is grown continuously through the year, because that keeps both the virus and the insect alive in the field.

The virus cuts yield by stopping the plant from making panicles. Researchers in the Philippines also found a strain of the virus that causes tungro like symptoms and can attack varieties that carry resistance genes. So farmers should watch for the signs along with the planthoppers. A related planthopper virus is [rice ragged stunt](/diseases/rice-ragged-stunt).

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: It can strike at any growth stage but hurts most at tillering, and it is worst where rice grows all year round and brown planthoppers never run out.
Brown planthoppers carry the virus. They must feed on a sick plant for at least 30 minutes to pick it up, and signs show 10 to 12 days after infection.

blocks.text: How to Identify Rice Grassy Stunt

Look for plants that stand upright, look short and grow many thin tillers, like a clump of grass. The leaves are yellowish green, shorter and narrower than normal, and they carry many small rusty spots that join into patches. A plant hit in the seedling stage rarely reaches maturity. A plant hit later may survive but makes no panicle. The signs can resemble tungro, so look for planthoppers at the base of the plants to help tell them apart.

items: Plants are severely stunted, with many thin tillers and a grassy, rosette look.
Leaves are yellowish green, shorter and narrower than normal.
Small rusty spots or patches cover the leaves and join into blotches.
Plants fail to make panicles, or make very few.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Grassy stunt looks like [rice tungro](/diseases/rice-tungro) and like rice yellow dwarf, because all of them stunt the plant and turn leaves yellow. Grassy stunt is the one with the grassy, rosette growth and rusty spots. Tungro is carried by green leafhoppers, not by brown planthoppers.
How Rice Grassy Stunt Hurts Your Palay

Grassy stunt reduces yield by stopping panicle production, so a hit plant gives almost no grain. A plant infected at the seedling stage seldom reaches maturity. The tillering stage is the most open to infection. We did not find a sourced yield loss percentage for the Philippines, so we give none here.

The virus has no cure. A sick plant stays sick, and the planthoppers that fed on it carry the virus on to the next plant. Because of that, the fight begins with the insect. In 2017 the brown planthopper resurged across 18 provinces, and the two viruses it carries, ragged stunt and grassy stunt, have no cure.
How to Control Rice Grassy Stunt

items: Plant a variety that resists the brown planthopper. Resistant varieties are the most reliable tool against planthoppers in the tropics.
Plant when the farms around you plant, so the insect cannot hop from older fields onto young ones. Synchronized crop establishment is one of the controls.
Avoid close planting, and leave a wider gap in the field every few meters so you can scout and so air can move.
Natural enemies keep planthoppers in check, such as spiders, mirid bugs, water striders and egg parasite wasps. Protect them by skipping early insecticide sprays.
Pull out and bury sick plants early, and plow under infected stubble after harvest, because the virus lives on in stubble and volunteer rice.
Drain and flood the seedbed for a day when planthoppers are present, so that the insects drown.

blocks.text: No spray can treat the virus in a sick plant. Insecticides target only the planthopper that carries it. Do not spray in the first 30 to 40 days after transplanting unless a pest is truly at outbreak level, because early sprays kill the spiders and wasps and cause planthopper outbreaks. If an outbreak is real, ask your local agriculture office which FPA registered product to use, and follow the label.

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different fungicide group next time, so the disease does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to plant diseases](/diseases/plant-diseases-philippines) explains how.

items: Plant a variety that resists the brown planthopper, or the virus, or both.
Plant together with the farms around you and keep a fallow, so hoppers cannot move from old fields onto young ones.
Pull out and bury sick plants early, and plow under stubble, ratoons and volunteer rice after harvest.
Flood the seedbed for a day when planthoppers are on it, so they drown.
No insecticide in the first 30 to 40 days, and never a pyrethroid: both bring planthoppers back worse.
Avoid close planting, and leave a narrow walking gap every few meters to scout.
Spiders, mirid bugs, water striders and egg wasps keep planthoppers in check. Spare them by not spraying early.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Rice Grassy Stunt

items.q: Is there a cure for rice grassy stunt?
items.a: No. The disease cannot be cured. You can only control the brown planthopper, use resistant varieties and remove sick plants early.

items.q: How soon do the signs show after infection?
items.a: Symptoms appear about 10 to 12 days after infection.

items.q: Should I spray right after transplanting?
items.a: No. Early sprays kill the spiders and wasps that keep planthoppers down. Spray only at a true outbreak and with advice from your agriculture office.
